turns.q: Is Supertech Supernova Astralis in Sector 94 on track for possession, and what is the risk if it slips?
turns.answer:
Supertech Supernova Astralis, Sector 94, Noida: Possession outlook and delay risk

The key question is whether Supertech Supernova Astralis will actually deliver on its promised possession date, rather than simply remain under construction. For a buyer or investor, that distinction matters because a delay can affect rental income, resale value, loan interest and the ability to recover money from the developer.

I would assess this project on three things: its latest construction progress, the possession date recorded with UP RERA, and the legal and financial position of the Supertech group. A possession date quoted by a sales team is not, by itself, proof that handover is on track.

1. Is possession on track?

My assessment: No—not safely enough to rely on a promised possession date without further verification. The risk is high.

The most important evidence is the official UP RERA record for Astralis itself, not just the wider Supernova residential complex.

Official RERA status

Supernova Phase III (Astralis – Commercial)

Registration: UPRERAPRJ7263

Declared completion date: 31 December 2018

Project status shown: Ongoing

Source: 
UP RERA official portal 
. 
UP RERA
+1

Developer and project-level risk

Supertech Realtors is undergoing insolvency proceedings, and a court-appointed committee has been working on a route to bring in a new developer for Supernova. 
The Indian Express
+1

There is a caveat: some property portals advertise Astralis as “ready to move,” and listings show different possession dates. That conflicts with the official RERA record. A portal listing is not proof that your particular unit has a valid occupancy/completion certificate or is legally ready for handover. 
MagicBricks
+2

2. What is the risk if possession slips?

Further delay: High risk

Insolvency proceedings, the process of selecting a new developer, funding and approvals can all push timelines out. A new developer being identified does not mean construction or handover will immediately follow.

Financial loss: Medium to high

You could face continuing loan interest, maintenance or holding costs, and lost rent or business income. If the space is intended as an investment, delayed cash flow can materially reduce the return.

Legal and handover risk: High

Physical access to a unit is not necessarily the same as lawful possession. Check the applicable occupancy/completion certificate, title or sub-lease documentation, fire approvals and access to common facilities.

Resale and exit risk: Medium to high

Uncertainty over handover, documentation and the developer's insolvency can narrow the pool of buyers and make resale slower or require a discount.

The legal position matters, too. Depending on your agreement, payment history, the nature of the delay and the insolvency proceedings, you may have remedies under RERA or other applicable law. However, a right to compensation or refund does not guarantee quick recovery of the money when insolvency is involved.

3. What has changed recently?

There is some positive movement toward resolving Supernova, but it should not be confused with a confirmed possession schedule.

May 2026: The Supreme Court-appointed committee selected PwC as transaction adviser to help identify and onboard a new developer for Supernova. 
The Indian Express
+1

September–October 2026: Court-supervised efforts to resolve Supertech's stalled projects have continued, but tribunals have raised concerns about missed deadlines and sought clearer project-level completion timelines. 
Company News - Business Standard
+1

For Astralis specifically, I could not verify a new, firm possession date backed by an updated official completion schedule. The RERA record still lists the project as ongoing.

4. What I would verify before buying or making another payment

Occupancy and completion certificates: Obtain copies and verify that they cover the specific Astralis tower and your unit.

Court-approved transaction status: Check whether the Supreme Court-appointed committee has approved the proposed sale or transfer. A public notice requires prior written approval for transactions involving Supertech Realtors' Supernova project. 
ETLegalWorld.com
+1

Construction and services: Inspect the actual unit, lifts, fire systems, electricity, common areas and access arrangements.

Your contractual protection: Have a property lawyer review the allotment agreement, payment schedule, delay-compensation provisions and your position in the insolvency process.

Written handover commitment: Ask for a date tied to specific milestones, not a verbal assurance from a broker.

The official 
UP RERA project record 
 and 
Supertech insolvency information portal 
 are the best starting points.

My bottom line

I would treat Supertech Supernova Astralis as a high-risk possession and legal-due-diligence proposition, not as a routine ready-to-move purchase. The court-supervised resolution process offers hope, but the evidence does not justify assuming that possession will happen on a reliable, near-term schedule.

One important distinction could change this assessment substantially:

Are you considering an office unit in Astralis, and has the seller told you that possession is already available or promised a future date? The answer will help distinguish a delayed handover from a unit that is physically accessible but still has unresolved approvals or title issues.

turns.q: Can I trust Supertech as a builder? What happened with their delayed projects?
turns.answer:
Can you trust Supertech as a builder?

My advice is to be very cautious about buying a Supertech property, especially if it is under construction or being sold at a discount because of delayed delivery. Supertech's history of project delays, financial distress and insolvency proceedings means that you should evaluate the specific project, not just the builder's name or the advertised price.

The important distinction is that a delayed project is not necessarily abandoned, and a builder's financial problems do not automatically mean every property it developed is defective or legally compromised. What matters is whether the particular project has a viable path to completion, clear title and a realistic possession timeline.

What happened to Supertech's delayed projects?

There are four major developments that explain the situation.

1. Projects remained incomplete for years

Supertech sold homes across the NCR during the 2010s, but many buyers did not receive possession on schedule. Some buyers have waited for more than a decade. Eco Village 1 and 2 in Greater Noida West are prominent examples. 
Delhi News - The Indian Express
+1

2. Supertech entered insolvency in March 2022

Supertech Limited was admitted to the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) on 25 March 2022. This brought its financial and project-completion problems into a formal insolvency process, involving creditors, homebuyers and court-supervised proceedings. 
Official Information Portal
+1

3. NBCC was brought in to help complete stalled projects

On 12 December 2024, the NCLAT approved a framework involving state-owned NBCC as project management consultant for 16 unfinished Supertech Limited projects. The Supreme Court upheld this arrangement on 5 February 2026. This created a route toward completion, but it did not mean that all homes were immediately ready for possession. 
Legal News - The Indian Express
+1

4. Progress has continued to face setbacks

In September 2026, the NCLAT raised concerns over missed deadlines for restarting construction and directed the relevant authorities to address delays in appointing an interim resolution professional. Homebuyers continued to report inadequate progress across the 16 projects.

One distinction matters here: a completed, occupied Supertech apartment is a very different purchase from an unfinished apartment awaiting resolution. Also, a project's inclusion in the NBCC framework does not, by itself, establish that every tower or unit is covered on the same terms.

Should you buy a Supertech property now?

My assessment depends on what you are buying.

Ready-to-move flat with occupancy certificate (OC): Potentially worth considering, provided title, approvals, dues and the actual unit are verified.

Resale flat in an occupied society: Potentially less exposed to construction risk, but outstanding loans, litigation and transfer restrictions still need checking.

Under-construction flat in one of the 16 stalled projects: High uncertainty. Do not rely on a broker's verbal promise that NBCC will complete it soon.

Cheap unit in a project with no clear completion plan: Treat the discount as compensation for risk, not automatically as a bargain.

Five checks to make before paying

Check UP RERA. Search the exact project and registration number for its registration status, completion date, extensions and orders.

Check the official insolvency records. Establish whether the particular project is covered by the court-approved completion framework and what the latest project-specific update says.

Verify the OC and completion certificate. For a supposedly ready flat, confirm that the relevant tower and unit are legally fit for occupation.

Get an independent property lawyer. Verify title, encumbrances, bank charges, litigation, outstanding dues and whether a sale or transfer requires approval.

Demand evidence of construction progress. Look for actual work on the relevant tower, an approved funding and completion plan, and a documented possession timeline.

Avoid paying a large non-refundable booking amount until these checks are complete. A bank's willingness to finance a property is useful information, but it is not a substitute for legal due diligence.

If your priority is builder safety, delivery risk, and protection of your money, I would compare Jaypee Klassic in Sector 134 and Gulshan Ikebana in Sector 143 on two separate questions: the financial/legal safety of the project and the quality of the building and maintenance.

My starting point would be to give greater weight to verified project-level records than to the builder's reputation or the apartment's appearance. In Noida, a project with a complicated land title, insolvency exposure, pending dues, or unclear completion documentation can be riskier even if the apartment itself looks good.

Five checks before paying a token

Occupancy certificate (OC): Obtain the actual OC from the relevant authority and verify that it covers your tower.

Title and registry: Have a property lawyer verify the chain of title, land lease, conveyance and the seller's right to sell.

Outstanding dues: Check Noida Authority dues, maintenance arrears, electricity charges and any mortgage or encumbrance affecting the flat.

Structural condition: Commission an independent inspection of seepage, cracks, lifts, fire systems, basement drainage and building maintenance.

Residents' feedback: Speak to at least three existing owners about water supply, maintenance, builder responsiveness, pending litigation and resale experience.

For Jaypee, I would additionally ask the lawyer to check whether the particular flat or tower is affected by any insolvency-resolution, possession or authority-related issue. For Gulshan, I would verify the exact tower's OC and registry eligibility rather than relying on the society's general ready-to-move status.

One question that could change my recommendation

Are you buying a ready-to-move resale flat for self-use, or buying primarily as an investment?

For self-use, I would lean towards Gulshan Ikebana, subject to document and inspection checks. For investment, the price difference, resale liquidity and expected rental yield could materially change which is the better purchase.
